answer:
1. The frames show a historical comparison of buying and renting in the US. The data sources are FHFA home prices, BLS rents and Freddie Mac mortgage rates. The grid has one tile for each possible start month, 247 in all, beginning in January 1991. Each tile is a buy-versus-rent outcome over a fixed holding period. Frames 5 and 6 add an illustrative character, Nina, standing between a house and an apartment building.

2. The holding period changes. Frame 3 is labeled "ten years" and shows a band of darker tiles in the grid. Frames 1, 2 and 4 are labeled "15 years" and show every tile in the same light color. The caption on frame 1 reads "15 years: every one (100%) · 247 start months". Frame 2 adds "weakest: $79,829 ahead". In frame 6 the rent tag on the apartment building is marked "unchanged".

3. At a 10-year horizon, some start months look different from the rest. Those are the darker tiles, which I take to be months where buying did not come out ahead. At 15 years, all 247 start months look the same, and the caption says buying came out ahead in every one. Even the weakest start month left the buyer $79,829 ahead. The "rent tag: unchanged" label seems to say that the renter's side of the comparison was held fixed. The frames don't show how this was calculated, and I'm reading the dark tiles as buying losing without a label saying so.

4. A viewer might conclude that buying has historically beaten renting over long holding periods, and that the longer someone stays, the more reliable that result gets. The frames don't say whether the viewer should buy. They say the data is "illustrative" and "US only · history, not a forecast".

5. The animation did not give advice, and the conclusion in 4 is mine. The on-screen text gives the "100%" and "weakest: $79,829 ahead" results. It also says the data is history, not a forecast, which cuts against reading it as a recommendation.
